title: Russia as a security actor in Central Asia: Losing primacy but retaining influence
text:
#### briefing paper

## Russia as a security actor in Central Asia

Kristiina Silvan

442November 2026

### Losing primacy but retaining influence

Summary

• Russia remains a central security partner for the Central Asian states despite its ongoing war in Ukraine. However, its position of primacy is eroding. China, Turkey, and other external actors have gained a foothold in the region’s security sector on terms set by Central Asian governments. 
• Russia’s arms exports to Central Asian states have decreased because of wartime demand and sanctions targeting its military-industrial sector. The region’s governments have responded by purchasing weapons from alternative partners, continuing a diversification trend that predates 2022. 
• Although the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) is marred by internal tensions, its infrastructure and Russia’s military facilities remain intact. Central Asian governments continue to participate in education and training activities offered by Russia, which in turn seeks to capitalize on its combat experience in Ukraine. 
• Finland and its EU and NATO partners should support the efforts of Central Asian governments to diversify their security partnerships. They can propose practical cooperation initiatives, especially in the areas of security education, human security, and environmental security. Such collaboration is, however, limited by the authoritarianism of the region’s governments and their close ties to Chinese and Russian actors. 

Author

Kristiina Silvan 
Postdoctoral Fellow 
Russia, Eastern Europe and Eurasia 
Finnish Institute of International Affairs 

##### Russia as a security actor in Central Asia

##### Losing primacy but retaining influence

BRIEFING PAPER 442 November 2026

Introduction

Amid Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, Moscow retains close ties with its Central Asian partners. While the governments in the region have categorically refused to endorse Russia’s invasion, they have also refrained from expressing explicit support for Kyiv. They have maintained that they comply with the sanctions imposed on Russia by the West but have argued that their compliance stems not from an endorsement of the sanctions but from their obligation to pursue their national interests.1 This diplomatic balancing act is hardly accidental. The economic ties between Russia and Central Asia remain substantial. Since 2022, remittances from Central Asian migrants working in Russia have increased rather than decreased, while Russian companies remain involved in strategically important sectors across the region, including nuclear energy.2

Yet some analysts also point to a tectonic shift in Russia’s regional position, from that of the “former hegemon” to that of “just another neighbour”.3

For years, Central Asian governments’ continued cooperation with Russia has gone hand in hand with a sustained and determined policy of strengthening

relations with all regional and global players. Since 2022, this diversification has accelerated across dif ferent policy spheres. According to many indicators, China has already become the region’s most influen tial external partner, while Western actors have also forged closer ties with the region’s capitals. This Briefing Paper focuses on Russia’s security role in Central Asia. It examines whether Russia has retained its position of primacy in the region’s security sphere despite its prolonged war in Ukraine. This position has traditionally been upheld by Russia’s military bases and installations, extensive connections between the armed forces and security services, weapons exports, and the provision of education and training.4 By mapping changes and continuities in Russia’s role in arms transfers, mili tary education, and the presence of Russian armed forces, the paper finds that the overall diversification of external partnerships is now extending to the sphere of hard security. As a result, Russia’s primacy in this sector is weakening, arguably both due to its focus on the war in Ukraine and to the choices made by Central Asian leaders. While Russia will most likely continue to play a pivotal role in the region’s security system for years, if not decades, to come, the newly diversified environment creates incentives for cooperation between EU and NATO countries on the one hand, and Central Asian actors on the other. This window of opportunity should be explored, bearing in mind that collaboration is constrained by the prevalence of authoritarianism and the region’s close ties to both China and Russia.

Russia’s role in the Central Asian arms trade

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the newly independent states of Central Asia each inherited some assets from the Soviet military. To ensure interoperability amid the economic downturn and the highly unstable security environment of the 1990s, all the governments in the region opted to import compatible weaponry from Russia and other countries of the former Soviet Union. This turned Russia into the dominant supplier of recorded major arms to the region in the 1990s.5 A significant share of this materiel was provided as aid in kind, making Russia the leading military donor to the region. Following the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the subsequent US-led war in Afghanistan, and against the backdrop of strengthening Central Asian economies, this picture started to change. The region witnessed an uptick in Western engagement, accompanied by increased military assistance and the transfer of equipment. For example, in 2001, the United States negotiated an agreement that allowed it to use Uzbekistan’s airspace and the Soviet-era Karshi-Khanabad airbase and pledged $55.7 million in foreign military funding to Central Asian govern ments for the subsequent year, almost two-thirds of which was allocated to Uzbekistan.6

At the same time, however, Russia’s monopoly on the Central Asian arms trade was solidified through new agreements on military-technical cooperation. The Collective Security Treaty Organ ization (CSTO) was established by Kazakhstan, Kyr gyzstan and Tajikistan, alongside Armenia, Belarus and Russia, in 2002 as an upgrade to the Collective Security Treaty of 1992. The organization created additional economic incentives for its Central Asian

members7 to continue relying on Russia as their primary arms supplier. In the 2010s, new suppliers emerged in the Central Asian arms market. China entered first as a donor and then as a commercial supplier. Its share of Central Asian arms imports rose almost tenfold during the 2010s, from 1.5% in 2010–2014 to 13% in 2015–2020.8 After the Second Karabakh War of 2020, Turkey’s Bayraktar TB2 drones were sought by all of the governments in the region – except for Kazakhstan, which signed an agreement to start manufacturing ANKA combat drones locally in partnership with Turkish Aerospace Industries.9 At the same time, however, overall trade volumes and cooperation in technical maintenance remained heavily tilted towards Russia. The CSTO member states of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan im ported almost all their weaponry from Russia, while Uzbekistan’s purchases from Russia accelerated as a result of a bilateral deal that allowed Tashkent to buy arms at Russian domestic prices. In the years before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia dominated arms supplies to the CSTO mem bers in Central Asia, whereas in the Uzbekistani and Turkmenistani markets, it was one supplier among others. According to the SIPRI Arms Transfers Database, the share of recorded major-arms imports measured by SIPRI trend-indicator value (TIV) from Russia in 2016–2021 stood at 90% for Kazakhstan, 88% for Kyrgyzstan, and 87% for Tajikistan. In contrast, Turkmenistan imported only 4% of its weaponry from Russia, compared with 40% from Turkey, 26% from China and 17% from Italy. With a 43% share of all transfers, Russia was the largest supplier of arms to Uzbekistan, while China ranked second, with its transfer of the FD-2000 air defence

However, as illustrated in Figure 1, the relative rarity of large transfers can easily skew the picture: in SIPRI’s 2018–2021 data, Russia’s dominance in Ka zakhstan’s arms imports is almost complete (97%), while in the case of Tajikistan, transfers from Russia are on a par with those from China. What is more, there is considerable variation in volumes: in the 2018–2021 period, the value of Russia’s transfers to Kazakhstan was over one hundred times higher than that of its transfers to Tajikistan. In the 2022–2025 period, however, the gap narrowed due to a nearly ninefold increase in the value of Tajikistan’s imports. Since the beginning of Russia’s war against Ukraine, arms transfers from Russia to Central Asia reported in the SIPRI database paint a mixed picture. The database records sizeable transfers to Kazakhstan in 2022, 2023 and 2024, but for the first time in over twenty years, SIPRI records no deliveries of major arms in 2025. For Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, single transfers are recorded in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan have reportedly received no arms transfers from Russia after 2021. Meanwhile, in 2022–2025, 19% of Kazakhstan’s arms imports came from NATO member states (France, Spain, Turkey, and others), and 41% of Kyrgyzstan’s imports came from Turkey alone. During the same period, China accounted for 96% of Tajikistan’s arms transfers and 67% of those to Uzbekistan.
